passage:
I still remember my first week in Rotterdam. The supermarket labels were unreadable, the bins had rules I broke on day two, and the flat was so quiet that I heard my own fridge. I felt free, I won't pretend I didn't, and also a bit unrooted, like a plant lifted with too little soil.
Damini, a colleague from the finance team, noticed me eating lunch alone and invited me to her Thursday dinner group. I nearly said no. I went. There I learned to cook a dish I had never heard of and taught them how to make my grandmother's tea.
I still call home every Sunday. Now I also have a Thursday. Both feel like mine.
Jagdish

qa.a: The narrator spent the first week in Rotterdam.

qa.a: Jagdish felt free but also unrooted and lonely, like a plant lifted with too little soil.

qa.q: What choice by Jagdish began to make the new place feel steadier?
qa.a: Jagdish nearly said no but accepted the invitation to the Thursday dinner group, and kept the Sunday calls home too.

qa.q: Why might Damini have invited Jagdish to the dinner group?
qa.a: Damini noticed Jagdish eating lunch alone and probably wanted to include a newcomer, and may have enjoyed learning about Jagdish's tea in turn.

grounding: A young adult moving abroad meets new rules and loneliness, and builds local friendships while keeping ties home.

Staff note, Toronto office, written by Vinita.
Vishal joined us in October from Hyderabad. In the first month he ate at his desk, rarely spoke in meetings, and told me that the cold and the food were a shock. He seemed capable but a little lost, though I cannot be sure what he felt.
What I did: I invited him to our Friday lunch walk and introduced him to Pedro from accounts, who plays weekend cricket with a group of locals. I also told him to keep his Sunday calls with his family, and offered to check the transit map with him for a route home.
Three weeks later, Vishal brought a home-made snack to the walk and was laughing with Pedro. I will keep our Friday check-in going for now.

qa.a: Vishal joined from Hyderabad.

qa.q: What did Vishal seem to be feeling in his first month?
qa.a: He seemed capable but a little lost and homesick, from the quiet meetings and his remarks about the cold and the food, though nobody can be sure of it.

qa.a: Vinita invited Vishal to the Friday lunch walk, introduced him to Pedro's cricket group, encouraged his Sunday calls home and offered help with the transit map.

qa.q: Why does the note say Vinita cannot be sure what Vishal felt?
qa.a: Vinita is careful not to treat his quiet manner as proof of his inner state, and only reports what was seen, such as the desk lunches and the later laughter.

"Tarun, I'm so tired of cold sandwiches."
"You've been in Toronto four months, Trisha Didi. You said it'd be an adventure."
"It is! I took the subway alone at night, and nobody stared. I wore shorts to work. I feel so free."
"Then why do you sound like this?"
"Because it's minus twenty and nobody here knows what rasam is. I ate dinner alone again. My colleagues are nice, but they go home at five."
"Have you tried inviting them?"
"...No."
"Then do. Cook rasam and make them try it."
"What if they hate it?"
"Then they hate it, and you laugh. At least you're not alone."
"Okay. Saturday. And I'll join that Sunday hiking group."
"Good. And call Amma tonight. She keeps asking."
"Every Sunday, I promise. I miss you, you know."
"I know. Go make rasam."

qa.a: Trisha feels free and adventurous, but also lonely and unrooted, eating dinner alone in the cold.

passage:
When I moved to Melbourne at twenty-four, I thought the hard part would be the job. It wasn't. It was Sundays.
I'm Mehak. The first months were wonderful: the trams, the ocean, the feeling of being unknown. Then winter came, and I realised I hadn't spoken to anyone outside work in two weeks. I video-called my mother every day, but hung up feeling worse, because home looked warm and I wasn't there.
Then a colleague, Gurpreet, invited me to the gurdwara's Sunday langar near her suburb. I'm not Sikh, but she said, "Nobody asks. Just come and help cut onions." I went. I cut onions for three hours and laughed more than I had in months.
Looking back, I needed both: the calls home, and the onions here. One kept me rooted. The other let me grow.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet invite Mehak?
qa.a: Gurpreet invited her to the gurdwara's Sunday langar near her suburb.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel after the daily video calls?
qa.a: Mehak felt lonely and homesick, hanging up feeling worse because home looked warm and Mehak wasn't there.

qa.q: What helped Mehak build a steadier life abroad?
qa.a: Joining Gurpreet at the langar gave Mehak local friendships and laughter, while calls home kept her rooted.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet see her invitation?
qa.a: Gurpreet probably saw it as a simple kindness, noticing a lonely colleague and welcoming her without any questions.

grounding: A young adult who moved abroad feels free but unrooted, and finds balance through local friendship while keeping ties with home.

passage:
Team lead's note, engineering office, Berlin, month two.
Nitin, 25, joined us from Pune in January. His work is excellent. But this month I noticed he eats lunch alone at his desk, leaves at five sharp, and looked grey on Monday mornings. He mentioned once that he'd spent the weekend "just sleeping," and that the supermarket rules confused him: bottles, bags, Sundays closed.
On Wednesday, Rukmini, from our data team, who moved from Chennai three years ago, invited him to her Friday cooking group, mostly other newcomers. He hesitated, then said yes.
Today he told me he'd cooked dal for eight people and learned the bottle-return system from a Ukrainian colleague. He also said he video-calls his parents every Sunday, "which keeps me sane."
Next step: I've asked Nitin to join our team's buddy programme for the next new hire.

qa.q: Who invited Nitin to the Friday cooking group?
qa.a: Rukmini, from the data team, invited him.

qa.q: What might Nitin have been feeling during his first months?
qa.a: Nitin was probably lonely and confused, eating alone, sleeping through weekends and puzzled by new rules.

qa.q: How did Nitin start building a steadier life?
qa.a: He joined Rukmini's cooking group to make local friends while keeping his Sunday video calls home.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have seen Nitin's situation?
qa.a: Having moved from Chennai herself, Rukmini likely recognised his loneliness and wanted to help.

grounding: A team lead's note shows a young adult abroad struggling with loneliness and new rules, and finding balance through local friends and ties home.

passage:
Chetan's diary. Toronto, Saturday, week 6.
Minus twelve today. I bought the wrong bus pass again, and the driver explained the zones very slowly, like I was a child, but kindly. Groceries cost what a week of dinners did at home. Nobody here asks where I'm from the way uncles ask; nobody asks anything. I like that. I also hate it.
At 4 pm I video-called Shankar and the whole gang at our old tea stall in Pune. They held the phone up to the rain. I laughed and then felt empty for an hour.
Then Mateo from the lab knocked. He'd made too much chili and said I looked like I needed beans. We ate on the floor and compared our mothers' cooking. He's from Monterrey, homesick too.
Tomorrow: the Sunday cricket group at the community centre. And call Aai.

qa.q: Where is Mateo from?
qa.a: Mateo is from Monterrey.

qa.q: What did Chetan feel after the video call with Shankar and the gang?
qa.a: Chetan laughed during it but then felt empty and homesick for an hour.

qa.q: What is Chetan doing to build a steadier life abroad?
qa.a: Chetan is accepting local friendship, like dinner with Mateo and the Sunday cricket group, while keeping ties home through calls to the gang and Aai.

qa.q: What might it be like for Mateo to knock on Chetan's door?
qa.a: Mateo, homesick too, probably wanted company as much as Chetan did, and sharing food eased loneliness for both.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult abroad facing new rules, costs and loneliness, feeling both free and unrooted, and building local friendships while keeping ties home.
